analysis.one_liner: Ends free mining on public land by charging royalties and fees, and funds cleanup of abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in May 2019 and never received a hearing or a vote; it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would overhaul the 1872 law that still governs hardrock mining (gold, copper, silver, uranium and similar minerals) on federal land. Today, companies can claim public land, take the minerals, and pay no royalty to the government, and can even patent — buy — the land outright. The bill would stop new land patents, charge a royalty of at least 5% of mining income, require permits and cleanup bonds before mining starts, and create a fund paid by the industry to clean up the hundreds of thousands of abandoned mines that leak pollution into western water. It never moved after its first day: it was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and sat there until the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who today bear the estimated multibillion-dollar cost of cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines; residents of western states and tribal communities whose rivers and groundwater are contaminated by mine drainage; and public-lands users, whose parks, wilderness study areas and roadless forests would be reviewed for protection from mining claims. Mining companies would pay royalties and fees, but the bill waives annual maintenance fees for small claim holders with 10 or fewer claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and western communities near mines

how_it_helps.text: Subjects hardrock mining on federal land to a royalty of 5–8% of gross mining income for the first time — under the 1872 law, companies remove these minerals without paying a production royalty.

Creates a Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund, financed by royalties, fees and an abandoned-mine fee, to reclaim land and water damaged by past mining, with priority for protecting public health and controlling mine water pollution.

Stops the government from granting patents — permanent private ownership of federal land — for any mining claim whose application was not filed by September 30, 1994, ending the practice of selling public land containing minerals at 19th-century prices.

Requires exploration and mining permits, reclamation plans, and financial assurance (bonds) sized to cover cleanup and long-term water treatment before mining can begin, so companies — not taxpayers — post the money for restoration.
Requires meaningful government-to-government consultation with Indian tribes before permits are issued for mining that could affect tribal lands or culturally significant areas.
Protects small claim holders: the $200 annual maintenance fee is waived for claim holders who hold 10 or fewer claims and have performed their assessment work.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, who would pay royalties for the first time, plus annual claim maintenance and location fees, land-use fees, and bonds covering full reclamation and long-term water treatment. The bill also carries a review of uranium development on federal land, and reviews of sensitive lands that could lead to new areas being withdrawn from mining.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the Interior Department to report on any impact of the royalties and fees on domestic mineral exploration and production — an acknowledgment that higher costs could reduce mining on federal land, with consequences for mining jobs and for domestic supply of minerals.
New permitting, bonding and inspection requirements would add upfront costs and time before a mine can start, which large companies can absorb more easily than small operators.

The royalty is grandfathered out for mines already operating under an approved plan of operations on the date of enactment, and the Secretary may grant royalty relief where production would not otherwise occur — so much existing production would continue paying nothing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main trade-off is between charging an industry that has mined federal land royalty-free for nearly 150 years, and the possibility that higher costs slightly reduce domestic mining. Against that: abandoned hardrock mines across the West pollute water and the cleanup burden currently falls on taxpayers, and the bill directs dedicated industry-funded money to that problem. The grandfathering of existing mines and the Secretary's discretion to lower royalties soften the bill considerably, which honest supporters would concede — the strongest provisions apply to new operations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 9, 2019 by Senator Tom Udall with eight Democratic cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

Under Senate practice, a bill cannot reach the floor unless its committee acts on it, so referral to a committee whose chair declines to schedule it effectively ends the bill; the 116th Congress expired on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: the 1872 mining law continues to let them extract gold, copper and other minerals from federal land without paying a production royalty, patent claims under the old grandfathering rules, and leave reclamation costs with taxpayers. Communities near abandoned mines continue to bear the pollution and cleanup costs.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose royalties, permits, bonding and a reclamation fund on hardrock mining on federal land.

for.name: 8 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors including Bennet, Heinrich, Markey, Wyden, Merkley, Booker, Harris and Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over federal mining law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 9, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, never brought the bill before the committee while it had jurisdiction, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats — while the Republican-chaired committee of jurisdiction never acted on the bill, and no Republican ever signed on.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver, uranium on federal land)
industries.note: For nearly 150 years these companies have paid no royalty for minerals taken from federal land and can claim the land itself. The bill would charge them 5–8% of mining income, annual fees, and reclamation bonds — real money that today stays with the companies while cleanup costs fall on the public.
Holders of 10 or fewer claims are spared the new maintenance fee if they perform their assessment work, but they still face the new permitting and bonding requirements for any non-casual activity.

industries.industry: States and Indian tribes with abandoned mines
industries.note: The bill lets qualifying states and tribes run their own reclamation programs and channels fund money to the 14 states with abandoned hardrock mines and to tribal land, addressing pollution that affects residents' water and health.
